summary: Defines criteria for judging an X.500 Directory System Agent implementation, including conformance to standards, performance, and demonstrated interoperability.

eli5.summary: A scorecard for grading directory software on rules followed, speed, and whether it works with others.

questions: how to benchmark x-500 directory software
subtitle: A scorecard for evaluating X.500 directory software on standards, features, and speed

tldr.problem: X.500 Directory System Agent (DSA) implementations vary widely in their conformance to standards, performance, features, and ability to interoperate, making it hard for organizations to choose and compare products.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1564 defines a comprehensive questionnaire with point scores covering protocol conformance, support for optional features, management tools, performance benchmarks, and demonstrated interoperability.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can use the metrics to evaluate DSAs suited to their needs—whether they prioritize speed, access control, schema flexibility, or commercial support—rather than trying to rank implementations by a single score.

facts.label: Point categories
facts.value: Conformance, features, performance, management, operational use, interoperability

facts.label: Scoring approach
facts.value: Category-based scoring; no single overall rank recommended

today: RFC 1564 is an Informational RFC from January 1994. X.500 directory deployments declined as organizations moved to Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and eventually cloud-based directory services. However, the metrics framework remains influential: similar evaluation approaches are used for other enterprise software. The RFC is historically significant for formalizing how to benchmark and compare complex infrastructure implementations fairly.

sections.title: What DSA Metrics Are
sections.content:
A Directory System Agent (DSA) is the software that implements the X.500 directory service, essentially a distributed address book and organizational database. While any X.500 DSA must conform to the standard to claim compatibility, conformance alone does not guarantee a useful implementation. Factors like query speed, throughput, ability to manage large databases, access control mechanisms, and support quality all matter.

RFC 1564 provides a framework of questions and point scores to measure DSA implementations across multiple dimensions: conformance to OSI standards, support for optional features like replication and access control, performance on typical operations, management capabilities, operational track record, and demonstrated interoperability. The metrics are organized by category so organizations can focus on what matters most for their use case.

Crucially, no single overall score is recommended. Different organizations have different priorities: some prioritize lookup speed, others require flexible schema management, still others need commercial support or proven deployments. The metrics allow comparison along whichever dimensions are relevant.
sections.eli5: This memo is like a checklist and scorecard for directory software. It asks: Is it fast? Does it follow the rules? Can you control who sees what? Does it work with other directory software? Has anyone actually used it successfully?

sections.title: Standards Conformance
sections.content:
The first major category is conformance to the X.500 and OSI standards. Questions cover implementation of the Directory Access Protocol (DAP) for clients connecting to a DSA, the Directory System Protocol (DSP) for DSA-to-DSA communication, and the abstract syntaxes required by X.519 (the core DSA specification).

Specific areas include whether the DSA supports all three levels of DAP (Read, Search, Modify), chained modes of operation, required authentication levels (anonymous, simple, protected simple, strong), and the full set of standard attribute types (X.520) and object classes (X.521). The RFC also asks about conformance testing conducted by the implementation's developers and support for implementor agreements like EWOS and GOSIP profiles.

Transport layer questions cover which underlying network protocols are supported: TP.4 over CLNS, TP.x over X.25, and for non-OSI environments, RFC 1006 (OSI over TCP/IP). Some implementations support lightweight inter-process communication for local clients to bypass the full protocol stack.
sections.eli5: This section asks: Does the software follow the X.500 rules? Does it handle all the kinds of directory operations? Does it use the right network protocols?

sections.title: Features and Extensions Beyond the Core Standard
sections.content:
Beyond basic conformance, many DSAs offer features introduced in the 1992/1993 revisions or developed independently. The RFC asks about support for RFC 1274 (COSINE and Internet X.500 schema), schema management (the ability to add or modify schema definitions), and dynamic schema compilation (whether changes require restarting the DSA).

Replication is assessed separately: does the DSA support replication as defined in the 1992 standard? Can it replicate individual entries, sibling groups, or entire subtrees? Are there alternative replication mechanisms in use?

Access control is crucial for multi-tenant and sensitive environments. Questions cover whether the DSA implements the 1992 standard access control model, allows users to maintain their own entries, supports role-based management rights, enables per-attribute protection, and implements advanced search/listing controls. Some implementations exceed the standard with additional features.

Additional questions cover RFC 1276 (distributed operations and replication), RFC 1006 compliance for non-OSI networks, and whether the DSA uses its own database or can integrate with commercial database packages like Oracle.
sections.eli5: This section asks: Can the software do extra things that the basic rule book does not require, like replicating copies to other locations, or controlling who can see which fields?

sections.title: Performance Benchmarking
sections.content:
The RFC defines a comprehensive benchmarking suite intended to give a realistic picture of DSA speed and throughput. All tests use a standard database of 20,000 entries below an organization node, subdivided into organizational units of varying sizes (10, 100, and 1,000 entries) with realistic attributes: common name, surname, telephone, postal address, and object class.

Tests measure operation latency and throughput under two conditions: a cold start where the operating system has not cached the database, and optimum conditions where caching benefits the implementation. This accounts for realistic deployment where repeated queries benefit from OS-level caching.

Specific operations timed include:

  • Bind: Time for a client to establish a directory session (separately for anonymous, simple, protected simple, and strong authentication).
  • List: Time to enumerate 10 or 1,000 sibling entries.
  • Search: Several search patterns on 100-entry and 20,000-entry subtrees (exact match, substring, approximate match, complex filters).
  • Read: Single entry retrieval.
  • Add, Modify, Modify RDN: Update operations with varying numbers of siblings.
  • Query rate: Throughput of repeated reads (list 100 entries then read each).

Implementers also document their test environment: hardware type, processor speed, memory, disk interface, operating system, network bandwidth, and protocol stack used, allowing reproducibility and adjustment for different hardware.
sections.eli5: This section defines speed tests. How long does it take to connect? To list entries? To search? To add an entry? And how fast can it handle many requests in a row?

sections.title: Real-World Use and Interoperability
sections.content:
Beyond lab tests, the RFC asks about operational evidence: the largest single DSA deployed, the largest set of interconnected DSAs supporting an organization, estimated number of organizations using the implementation, and commercial deployment scale.

Interoperability is demonstrated through documented participation in X.500 pilots (like the COSINE/Internet Pilot), testing with other implementations, and identified compatible systems. The RFC does not require perfect interoperability; it asks what has actually been tested and where the DSA is known to work.

Management tools are assessed: can administrators monitor DSA activity via DAP, CMIP, or SNMP? Are there tools for runtime control, knowledge base management, data consistency checks, or database arboriculture (moving, copying, deleting subtrees)?
sections.eli5: This section asks: Is this software actually used? Does it really work with other directory systems? Do administrators have tools to manage it?

sections.title: Practical Characteristics and Implementation Details
sections.content:
The RFC also captures practical implementation details that affect deployability. Questions cover maximum simultaneous associations (connection limit), maximum database size, entry sizes (both in memory and on disk), indexing support (can the database be fully inverted or indexed for specific attributes?), and the specific indexes that improve different search patterns (exact match, substring, approximate match).

The approximate match algorithm is asked about specifically, since implementations vary in their matching logic. Questions also cover whether the DSA uses relay DSAs (multi-homed nodes) to bridge networks, whether the start-up time is acceptable (with timing for a 20,000-entry database), and how indexing affects both performance and storage overhead.

These details allow an organization to estimate whether a particular implementation will fit their hardware constraints, performance requirements, and operational model.
sections.eli5: This section asks practical questions: How many people can connect at once? How many entries can it store? How long does it take to start up? How much disk space does it need? How much faster are indexed searches?
